clinicalPearls: Thrombosis is essentially hemostasis occurring in the wrong place at the wrong time; the same processes that protect against hemorrhage can, under certain conditions, produce pathologic arterial or venous occlusion.
Hemostasis and thrombosis arise from interplay among three elements: the vessel wall, the coagulation/fibrinolytic proteins, and platelets.

Arterial thrombosis is dominated by platelet adhesion to an injured vessel wall and the state of the wall itself, whereas venous thrombosis is driven mainly by activation of the coagulation cascade in the setting of stasis or hypercoagulability.
Platelets are small anucleate cells (1-5 microns) circulating at roughly 200,000-400,000/microL with a 7-10 day lifespan, derived from marrow megakaryocytes under the control of thrombopoietin.

The platelet GPIb-IX-V complex binds exposed subendothelial von Willebrand factor to initiate adhesion, and signaling converts the GPIIb/IIIa integrin from a low-affinity to a high-affinity fibrinogen receptor that cross-links platelets into an aggregate.

Inflammation and infection transiently raise thrombotic risk: acute upper respiratory infection, bacterial and viral infections (including SARS-CoV-2, HIV, hepatitis C, dengue) are linked to increased myocardial infarction, stroke, and VTE.
Roughly 5-8% of the U.S. population carries a genetic risk factor predisposing to venous thrombosis, and multiple risk factors frequently coexist in a single patient.
Cancer confers an approximately fourfold increased risk of VTE compared with the general population, and VTE in cancer patients is associated with reduced survival.

Although factor V Leiden and the prothrombin G20210A mutation are established risk factors for DVT and PE, their contribution to arterial thrombotic events such as acute coronary syndromes is not well established.

Loss-of-function CYP2C19 polymorphisms are the strongest single determinant of reduced antiplatelet response to clopidogrel (a prodrug requiring hepatic activation) but account for only about 5-12% of the variability in ADP-induced platelet aggregation.

Antithrombin reactions governed by normal endothelium become pivotal in limiting clot extension into adjacent uninjured vessel once a protective clot has formed; antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, heparin cofactor II, and protein C/protein S all restrain thrombin generation.
harrison.pathophysiology: Thrombus formation reflects dysregulated hemostasis involving the vessel wall, coagulation and fibrinolytic proteins, and platelets. In arterial thrombosis, vessel-wall damage exposes subendothelial collagen and von Willebrand factor; the platelet GPIb-IX-V complex mediates adhesion, platelets are activated through seven-transmembrane receptors (thrombin/PAR1, PAR4, ADP receptors P2Y1 and P2Y12, prostaglandin and lipid receptors), release thromboxane A2, serotonin, and ADP from granules, and undergo a calcium-dependent conformational change in GPIIb/IIIa that allows high-affinity fibrinogen binding and irreversible aggregation. Most arterial thrombi are superimposed on disrupted atherosclerotic plaque whose thrombogenic core triggers platelet-rich thrombus. In venous thrombosis, the coagulation cascade is initiated chiefly by exposure of tissue factor: factor VII/VIIa-tissue factor complex activates factor X (directly or via factor IX/VIIIa), FXa with cofactor FVa converts prothrombin to thrombin, thrombin converts fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin and activates FXIII to cross-link the clot. Amplification lets a small stimulus generate large amounts of fibrin. Venous thrombi typically originate in valve cusps of calf deep veins or muscular sinuses where sluggish flow lowers oxygen delivery, activating endothelial cells that express adhesion molecules; tissue-factor-bearing leukocytes and microvesicles adhere, neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) provide a scaffold that binds and activates platelets and activates factor XII, and impaired clearance of activated clotting factors worsens local thrombosis. Hypercoagulability (heritable or acquired), stasis, and vascular dysfunction (Virchow's elements) underlie venous events. Inflammation links the two: platelet P-selectin binds leukocyte PSGL-1, induces monocyte tissue factor and CD40 ligand expression, and Toll-like receptors (TLR2/3/4, TLR7/8) connect infection to platelet-dependent thrombosis.

nonInfectiousMimics: Acute limb ischemia from arterial embolism rather than local thrombosis
Lymphedema or cellulitis mimicking DVT-related limb swelling
Extrinsic venous compression mimicking thrombotic obstruction
additionalInvestigations: Thrombophilia evaluation (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin, protein C, protein S deficiencies) in selected patients, recognizing many older genetic associations are being questioned in larger contemporary studies
Antiphospholipid antibody testing when autoimmune prothrombotic state suspected
Plasma homocysteine and MTHFR considerations as historically reported independent risk factors
Assessment of acquired risk factors: malignancy screening, recent surgery/trauma, pregnancy status, hormonal therapy use
Markers reflecting inflammation-thrombosis crosstalk (e.g., soluble CD40 ligand) noted as research-relevant
redFlags: Sudden death from pulmonary embolism (a substantial fraction of new VTE cases die early, with high 30-day mortality)
PE in the setting of cancer carries roughly a 25% fatality rate
Homozygous protein C or protein S deficiency can produce fatal purpura fulminans
Coagulation abnormalities and increased PE/DVT/peripheral thrombosis in hospitalized COVID-19 patients (noted in nearly 20%)
Calf-vein thrombus extension into popliteal and proximal veins, where fragments can embolize to the lungs
harrison.prognosis: Thrombosis is a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Coronary disease and stroke account for a large share of deaths; arterial thrombosis underlies most acute MI, ischemic stroke, and limb gangrene. For VTE, up to 30% of patients die within 30 days, about one-fifth experience sudden death from PE, and roughly 30% develop recurrent VTE within 10 years. The ARIC study reported a 9% 28-day fatality from DVT and 15% from PE; cancer-associated PE carries about 25% fatality. Incidence of first DVT rises sharply with age (from about 2-3 per 10,000 person-years at 30-49 years to about 20 per 10,000 at 70-79 years). Increasing age, obesity, malignancy, and acute extremity paresis independently predict recurrence.
pitfalls: Assuming hypercoagulable (thrombophilic) states that drive venous thrombosis are equally important for arterial events; their role in acute coronary syndromes is poorly defined and often not clinically significant.
Genotyping to optimize aspirin therapy is not currently clinically indicated, as ex vivo studies have not firmly established a pharmacogenetic interaction between aspirin and COX1.

Over-relying on CYP2C19 genotype for clopidogrel decisions, since loss-of-function alleles explain only a small fraction (about 5-12%) of antiplatelet response variability and genetics do not appreciably affect outcomes with prasugrel or ticagrelor.
Forgetting that up to 10% of venous thromboembolic events occur outside the lower extremities and lungs.
Treating many older single-gene thrombophilia associations as definitive when larger contemporary studies have called several into question.
management: Antiplatelet therapy such as aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor is the mainstay for arterial thrombosis
Anticoagulation for venous thromboembolism, using heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin followed by a direct oral anticoagulant or a vitamin K antagonist
Acute reperfusion for arterial events, with thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy and revascularisation in myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke or acute limb ischaemia
Identify and treat an underlying prothrombotic state, and use a vitamin K antagonist rather than a direct oral anticoagulant in confirmed antiphospholipid syndrome
Modify risk factors, including smoking cessation, and review hormonal therapy contributing to venous risk
Individualise anticoagulation duration according to whether the event was provoked or unprovoked and the bleeding risk
Refer to haematology for thrombophilia evaluation in recurrent, unusual-site or unexplained thrombosis
